chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd, from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari, who said: Al-Rida (peace be upon him) said:
The Divine Will and the Divine Intent are among the Attributes of Action. So whoever claims that Allah, the Exalted, has always been the Intending Willer, then he is not a monotheist.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Divine Will and Divine Intent in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) distinguishes between Will (Irada) and Intent (Shi') as attributes of action (Sifat al-Fi'l), which are contingent upon the existence of their objects, rather than eternal attributes of essence. This clarification safeguards Tawhid against the Mu'tazila and others who might conflate divine will with eternal essence, ensuring that Allah's volition is understood as a timeless act of will rather than a newly acquired quality. The hadith thus reinforces the Shia doctrine that while Allah's will is eternal in its essence, its manifestation is relative to creation.

en.sayed-ali-raza-rizvi: 5. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (RA) said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan alSaffar said, on the authority of Muhammad ibn `Isa ibn `Ubayd, on the authority of Sulayman ibn Ja`far al-Ja`fari that Al-Rida (AS) said:
“The Divine Will and the Divine Intent are part of the Attributes of Action. So whoever claims that Allah, the Exalted, has always been the Intending Willer, then he is not a (true) monotheists.”
